title: The Factors that Affect Learning: Curriculum - a short introduction
author: Martin Skelton
summary: This short introductory post defines what Skelton means by curriculum before the following posts assess how it helps or hinders learning. He argues that curriculums exist everywhere in life, from re-wilding a garden to hosting visitors, and share the same components of outcomes, activities, resources and evidence of success. Some curriculums are explicit and some are held in the head, and the hidden curriculum shows how unplanned repeated experiences teach things nobody intended. He reduces a curriculum to five elements: what is to be learned, what is assessed, what activities are experienced, what resources are needed and what evidence shows success. The idea of curriculum is generally good, he says, but real curriculums vary widely in how well they help learning happen. He promises checklists and states he will not recommend any particular curriculum.
points: Curriculum is defined simply as planned and guided learning with outcomes, activities, resources and evidence, so the concept applies far beyond schools.
Explicit versus informal curriculums matter because what is kept hidden can quietly teach the wrong lessons.
The hidden curriculum is illustrated by the author's own unplanned half hour of faffing each morning, which taught his class something about learning that he never intended.
Curriculum quality is judged by how well it supports repeated experiences, good struggle and stickiness, not by its mere existence.
Skelton deliberately refuses to recommend a curriculum, positioning the choice as the school's own responsibility.
quotes: Curriculums are not just something you find in schools. We all have curriculums for much of our personal and professional lives, even if we don’t think of them as such.

We had outcomes for our re-wilding project. We’d be able to look at those outcomes and both assess and evaluate whether we had been successful. We had some activities that, if we did them well, would hopefully lead to us achieving our outcome. We had a sort of timescale over which we would do all this. All of these things are components of many educational curriculums.
None of this was ‘intended’ on my part and faffing about certainly wasn’t written down anywhere, but my class’s negative learning about learning still happened.
Something has to guide all that just as something guides our garden re-wilding, the visits of our friends, and my longer than usual run this morning. That something in schools is the curriculum.
Curriculum’ as an idea is usually good, but actual curriculums in practice vary in quality and definitely vary in the extent to which they really help learning to happen.
It’s very rare - not impossible, but rare - for curriculums to be wholly helpful to learning or wholly unhelpful to learning. Our trick is to try and make them more rather than less helpful.
The next few posts won’t be recommending any particular curriculum to you. Choosing or recommending a curriculum is not my job; it is yours to make in your own school or your organisation.
